speechtext:
Let me get back to Poland. Solidarity was supposed to be 12 million strong. Perhaps in spirit, but I do not think in fact. Solidarity has collapsed. Prime Minister Woj-ciech Jaruzelski declared a state of emergency. Lech Walesa and approximately 10,000 Solidarity members and even the former party leader, Edward Gierek, were imprisoned. That is the situation.
To understand how Poland got to this position, you have to understand the history of Poland. Poland has had almost 1,000 years of wars, splits and divisions going back to the year 966. That was when supposedly-it may-be myth-the first king of Poland, King Miezko, ruled. Poland progressed into the sixteenth century. That was supposed to be the golden age of Poland. 1 think it was. In the sixteenth century Poland was the predominant power in eastern Europe. In 1572 the Jagellonian dynasty died out. It had existed from the fourteenth century to the sixteenth century. What is odd about that and why Poland declined is something that we should remember in Canada. More and more power was given to the landed gentry. In 1652,
Supply
the notorious liberum veto was introduced. This situation has almost come into being in Canada. Any member of the Diet could defeat legislation. Doesn't that sound like the power given to the provinces? This liberum veto could nullify previous laws and it could dissolve the Diet.
By the mid-seventeenth century Poland was in its decline. The Russians invaded from the east and the Turks came from the west. The Cossacks living in the frontier area of Poland revolted and Charles X of Sweden invaded Poland. I tell hon. members opposite to listen and learn. They will learn something about the country they are talking about. I say to hon. members: "Do not form your foreign policy on what happened last week by what is reported in The Globe and Mail." I tell them to learn something about what makes Poland tick.
In 1660 Poland had peace. But wars, the bubonic plague and mass murders followed and by 1668 the population was reduced to 4 million. It had decreased 55 per cent. The cities lost all their manufacturing, most of their industries and three quarters of their inhabitants.
Between 1704 and 1710 Poland went to war with Sweden. Sweden invaded Poland and one third of the Polish cities were in ruins. Between 1702 and 1710 the population decreased from 8 million to 6.4 million. Sweden advanced into the Ukraine and Russia defeated Sweden. Under Peter the Great, Russia took over Poland.
Hon. members have to understand the historical connection between Russia and Poland. In 1763 Catherine's former lover, Stanislas Pontiatowski, was made King of Poland. Finally Poland died as a result of three partitions. These partitions occurred in the years 1772, 1793 and 1794. Poland was divided in 1975. Russia, Prussia and Austria took over the country and Poland totally disappeared. This was the First time in the history of Europe that a country by cold calculation was divided up and disappeared without war.
However, during this period there was a group much like Solidarity today. It was led by a peasant called Kosciuszko. They had only scythes as weapons but they defeated the Russians at Raclawice. If it had not been for the Prussians coming to the aid of the Russians, the Poles might have been successful. Except for one period under Napoleonic rule, Poland disappeared until after World War I when we come into modern history.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Poland was created from three defeated empires after 1918. But even then the Poles seemed to do the wrong thing. In 1920 Poland went to war against Russia. The Poles were governed by a band of colonels who were cronies. They had fought against Russia in World War I. Poland went through a period under Marshal Pilsudski. Marshal Pilsudski said something interesting about Poland. He said: "Even if you are defeated, if you are not vanquished, that is victory." That seems to be the Polish phenomenon that we witness. Poland basically went through a series of benevolent dictatorships prior to World War II. But in this period Poland attacked Lithuania over a dispute concerning the city of Vilna.

Poland attacked Czechoslovakia and Poland again attacked Russia.
In World War II Poland would not aid Czechoslovakia nor would it allow Russian troops to cross Poland to aid Czechoslovakia. William L. Shirer said that "this was bound to be a policy of suicide".
And that is what it turned out to be. Poland alienated all of its allies surrounding it. Mr. Shirer went on to say:
-and indeed it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the Poles in the nineteen thirties, as on occasions in the centuries before, were & 1700;-1 driven by some fateful flaw in their national character toward self-destruction and that in this period, as sometimes formerly, they were their own worst enemy.
After World War II Poland was basically under the absolute rule of Russia. But it was not until 1955 that Poland became a member of the Warsaw Pact. In this respect, it is interesting to note what happened.
At the beginning of World War II Russia made a secret pact with Germany. The Russians moved into the eastern half of Poland. In this connection 6 million Poles died, which represented almost 22 per cent of the population. There were over 600,000 war casualties. Poland sustained damage to its industry, its communications, its housing. Damage sustained to Polish culture was impossible to estimate. Toward the end of World War II, on August 1, 1944 there was still that will, that search for freedom, within the people and the Polish underground arose. Poland was still occupied. The underground movement lasted two months. The Russians incited the uprising, but they did nothing to help. The Poles were virtually wiped out by the Germans. Two hundred thousand people, mostly young boys and girls, were killed by German SS troops as revenge.
Finally, on January 17, 1945 the Russians took over, and unlike other countries such as Yugoslavia and Albania, which were liberated by their own partisan communists, Poland was liberated along with Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, East Germany and Czechoslovakia and occupied by Russia.
You cannot call that liberation.

Eventually through a process of elimination the communist party took over in Poland. In 1948 the Socialist party and the Polish workers' party emerged to become the Polish united workers party. The Stalin purges occurred between 1947 and 1949. In 1955 Poland became a member of the Warsaw Pact.
Throughout 1000 years of autocratic history there have always been groups in Poland who have searched for freedom. There was the peasants' revolt under Kosciuzko. Solidarity was led by Lech Walesa and there were the World War II freedom fighters. Truly, to be defeated without being vanquished, that is victory.
After World War II and a slow start as a result of its aftermath, and during the cold war period, Canada's relations with Poland developed comparatively quickly, especially during the 1960s and into the heydays of detente of the 1970s.
As the minister said, we have maintained that the internal problems of Poland must be solved by the Poles themselves. But we want to impress upon Polish authorities that their actions are met with categorical disapproval by most of the Canadian people.
The hon. member for St. John's West I believe has said "do something". He keeps leading up to it but I am never sure what he means. I think he said: "Cut off our exports of grain to Poland". What else is there?
I never said that. Read the March 24 statement and see what was suggested.

I am getting a little tired of criticisms about what we have or have not done for Poland. Right now we have allocated $500 million of credit to Poland. This is the highest per capita of any western democracy. Also we have allowed 1.5 million tonnes of grain to be shipped to Poland on credit and have allocated $500,000 to the International Red Cross for food, clothing and medical supplies. This is what we have done. I am getting sick and tired of opposition members not acknowledging these facts. Tell the facts as they are. Canada and Canadians have been the most generous per capita in the world as far as Poland is concerned.
That is Canada's commitment to the Polish people. But is it enough? As John Stuart Mill said in 1854:
The worth of a state, in the long run, is the worth of the individuals composing it ... A state which dwarfs its men in order that they may be more docile instruments in its hands even for beneficial purposes, will find that with small men no great thing can really be accomplished-

This government seems prepared to send nuclear bundles to the enemy of that country so that it can develop nuclear energy.

I am sure the minister-he may be the only one or there may be others, such as the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne)-has heard of San Carlos de Bariloche, a famous ski resort in the Andes, in southwest Argentina and adjacent to the Chilean border. It is a ski resort but it is also the seat of the Argentinian think tank. As well, it is a detainee centre where Argentinians used to send political detainees, such as Evita Peron, at one time. There were possibly others detained there.
It may be that the Argentinians had in mind to take over the Falkland Islands and transport detainees from San Carlos de Bariloche to the Falkland Islands where they could be safety left. I am referring to those people which Argentina would not want to have in its own country. They would not be able to swim back to the mainland in order to cause trouble. It would be sort of a Devil's Island for Argentina.
Another thing which happens at San Carlos de Bariloche- and I am sure the minister knows this-is that it is the Argentinian atomic research centre. This is where research goes on, using spent fuel or plutonium created from the use of the Candu reactor, likely to process a nuclear device. We all remember what happened in India. We had an ironclad guarantee that there would be no bomb construction, and then we heard that India managed to create one. San Carlos de Bariloche in southwest Argentina is a centre where this work could likely be conducted. The government now has an opportunity, with the action of the dock workers or stevedores in Saint John, to reconsider its actions and say that it will not send these rods to Argentina where they might be misused, despite the undertaking which has been given.
There are two other areas which I wish to raise in deploring the actions, policies and performance of the government. There is so much which is deplorable about the foreign policies and performances of this government that one barely knows where to start. I will give one instance.
Almost two years ago an initiative was taken by the Institute of Natural Resources in Pietermaritzburg in Natal, South Africa, to work up an exchange of persons and ideas with a department in the Ontario government on land use programs in Natal and in one of the Bantustan states of Kwazulu. The South African institute felt that Ontario had much to offer in this area and was anxious to draw on Ontario's experience.
The concepts that were being explored were not only innocuous in political terms but could well form the basis of useful interchanges in areas of great importance to both countries. They included the development of what is called the integrated approach to land use. That is, use based on a sound evaluation of the natural resources of a region plus a thorough understanding of the people's needs and wants in that region. These were purely technical studies and a prospective useful interchange approved wholeheartedly by the South African government.

By January, 1981, the plans had matured to the point where an exchange of scientists was being considered. The names were almost ready. A Canadian was to go to South Africa to explore related techniques as developed in Canada and a South African was to come to Canada to the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources where he could see what there was transferable from Canada in technology to South Africa. Everything seemed to be in place for this exchange of officials. 1 underline the word "officials". They were not politicians or soccer players or rugby players, but technical officials.
Only a month later, in February, 1981, the whole deal was off. Why? The Ministry of Natural Resources of Ontario had said that they were in touch with the Canadian Department of External Affairs in Ottawa and, believe it or not, they were advised, and I quote from the letter:
Since we wrote to you last October, 1 have been in contact with the Canadian Department of External Affairs in Ottawa. I have been advised that a cooperative project between the government of Ontario and the Government of South Africa through your Institute would be inappropriate in light of the present state of relations between Canada and South Africa.
What was so harmful and inappropriate about such an interchange? But they said it would be inappropriate, and the province of Ontario bowed to the superior knowledge of the Department of External Affairs. I believe it is a sad comment on international relations and the manner in which this government handles those relations.
The other area I wish to speak on relates to the report prepared at the behest of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) by Miss Pamela McDougall who is a former ambassador to Poland and a high ranking civil servant since her return from Poland. She was to look into what is called "conditions of the foreign service".
Programs affecting External Affairs have struck me as being deplorable for a long time. I would say that the most deplorable programs began about 1968, but even before then. I can recall as far back as the mid-1960s when managerial reorganizations were imposed on the department with little or no prior consultation by people who had little or no notion of what a foreign office was designed to do. "Experts" were brought in from outside to reorganize a department whose function within the Canadian government service and whose function within the world these experts were absolutely incapable of understanding.
The net effect of that reorganization, or those reorganizations, were that the employees of the firm which had been sent in to reorganize the department found niches for themselves in the department and settled in. Eventually they moved up into the higher positions. They liked External Affairs the way it was and they were determined to enjoy some of the fruits of overseas service. They were not equipped or trained in the foreign service. They came in as managerial experts.
Now, we find that Miss McDougall discovers that the Department of External Affairs is in a managerial shambles. This shaking up of the department was just getting under way when the bilingualism program was introduced with all that it meant in absences from foreign policy desks. I might add that
this bilingualism program was introduced to a department which was at that time, I am quite sure, more bilingual than any other department in the Canadian government.
This was almost immediately followed by a scheme of "program budgeting" and subsequently by "zero based budgeting." Shortly after that we were involved with absorbing all overeas support staff into the staff of the Department of External Affairs. We then had to contend with the problems of lateral entry. The early Ericksons of this world were being brought in to the Department of External Affairs at fairly high levels while preventing promotion up through the ranks. We then learned about the interdepartmental interchange from one department to the other which was presumably to reflect the government's notion of what Canada is.
As though this were not enough, there was a scheme for consolidation thrust upon the department by the Prime Minister's office. Then almost immediately there was the appointment of Miss McDougall to look into what was described as conditions in the foreign service. You can be sure that conditions by this time were in a sorry state and a royal commissioner such as Miss McDougall was needed to look into those conditions.
What is deplorable about how the government functions is that no sooner had the McDougall report been submitted in October of 1981 that a further and a more comprehensive consolidation of all the departmental officers from all departments concerned with offshore and overseas problems relating to trade, immigration and foreign policies-but not CIDA- were to be integrated into the Department of External Affairs with three ministers superimposed on them. Is it any wonder that the Department of External Affairs had been going through a period of the jitters, as it most certainly has? This can be verified if you talk to the employees of the department. It was so deeply involved in reorganizing itself and its departmental structures and learning about all the different kinds of budgeting and remanipulation of streams of command that it had little or no time to turn to the fundamental problems for which the department was established, that is, the definition of foreign policy recommendations for the government.
Due to these manifold and concurrently imposed changes, it has been obliged to be, at best, responsive to outside events and by no means capable of developing new initiatives to further Canada's causes in the many fields of our concern. Perhaps this is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) wants. I can recall as far back as the mid-1960s when he was quoted as saying: "What is the use of sending all those types to missions abroad? We can read what is going on in the world by reading The New York Times." I see a former foreign service officer walking behind the curtain. He could confirm this fact if he would stand up and say so. What the Prime Minister failed to take into account in such a cynical, arrogant and indeed stupid and ignorant comment was that, without a fully trained and devoted foreign service, it is just not possible to get to the bottom of the motivations of peoples and states except through living abroad.
June 1, 1982

What is it that causes them to adopt this stand or that at the United Nations, or in a disarmanent debate, or in the Law of the Sea discussions or to invade the Falklands? These matters do not develop overnight. They can be observed only by a competent foreign service. These in-depth analyses of motivation and explanation of national behaviour are not to be found in news reports, in The New York Times or any other paper, despite what the Prime Minister says. That is what the Department of External Affairs was well trained to do, until successive governments under this Prime Minister deliberately debilitated it and set out to destroy that essential capacity in foreign affairs.
Why otherwise, 1 ask myself, did Miss McDougall feel moved to recommend as she did in her report at page 55? Recommendation 44 is a very important recommendation and I implore your Honour to listen. It states, "Concrete steps should be taken to correct the widely held view that those in positions of power consider the activities and the product of the foreign services largely irrelevant to federal government or Canadian objectives." When a royal commissioner has to make that kind of a recommendation, conditions in the foreign service are in a sorry state. They are at a low ebb. I am glad that there are at least two ministers present in the House to hear my comments.

Mr. Speaker, my contribution to this debate will be fairly well directed to one aspect, and that is by way of an overview to the background of Polish history to indicate what is expected of that country today and in what direction our help and our support should be given. Much of the debate, a great deal of the talk that one hears and the arguments put forward are without a real understanding of what the underlying cause of the problem has been in Poland. The help being given is very much that of symptomatic relief. It is superficial help. It does not get down to the cause of the internal and worrisome problem existing in that country.
To really understand it, one must look back to Yalta in 1945, at which time the principals, namely Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill, made a decision by which Poland was handed to Russia. It was put under the sphere of influence of Russia with the rather vague understanding that within the next one or two years, a free election would take place and at that time the country would be given an opportunity to direct its future. This was an assurance given by two allies, by Churchill and President Roosevelt.
This was a very damaging and unbelievably serious blow to the personality of that particular nation. Until that point,
Supply
Poland had a record of one thousand years as a protector of the Christian faith. It had been a protector of democratic principles. It had contributed to the world of art and to the world of music. It had been scholarly in various intellectual pursuits. At that time it was the centre of university training and had the ultimate example of the concepts of freedom and education. This freedom, by virtue of that meeting at Yalta, was snatched away.
Those of us who took part in the last war heard stories of the exploits of the Polish people in a military sense. They took a very active part in the Royal Canadian Air Force. Indeed, a prominent member of this House from Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) was a member of that squadron and took part in some of the air battles. The Poles made a very outstanding defence at Monte Cassino in Italy under Alexander. They fought in Africa in the third Canadian and British divisions under Montgomery and acquired the distinction of being very worthy fighters and supporters of the allied cause.
What I am pointing out is that this country, whose ideals and ideology were similar to ours, and which supported the Christian faith, was handed over to a completely foreign country with an ideology completely incompatible with its personality, background, ideals and hopes. It was at that point that if anyone were to assist the Poles, they ought to have stepped forward. Unfortunately, there was no initiative by any of the allied countries to give the Poles that free election and the opportunity to acquire the status they had previously held. What happened was that this nation of courageous and hardworking individuals was able to adjust on its own, and did adjust, to the conditions under which it was forced to live.
Shortly after 1945, the Poles did accept a socialist form of government and the loss of sovereignty and were prepared to work with the communist government imposed on them. They realized very early that they comprised a buffer state between western Europe and the eastern communist bloc. However, their spirit and drive were such that they were not satisfied.
All of us who have followed the progress of the country of Poland have seen how it was possible for the unions to be organized under the very eyes of the communist regime, how they were united with the support of the church, the farmers and the university students. The Polish people formed a union which was unique in the world, one which worked hand-inhand with management, with the academics and with the farmers in creating a force which, through its own moral suasion, was able to bring ten million of their 14 million workers under one umbrella unit.
The members of this group known as Solidarity were effective in producing a crack in the ideological makeup which we know as communism, and they have continued to enlarge that crack. They were able to surround themselves with people of similar aims amongst the Czechoslovakians and the Hungarians, and then martial law was imposed upon them. Now,

my message is just simply this: that the underlying disease, the deep-seated, deep-rooted problem, the gnawing cancer that exists is their loss of freedom, the loss of their individuality, their loss of hope in the future. This is the primary problem which at this point has no ready cure, no easy approach. However, they do require the understanding of other democratic countries about them. They do require a constant representation on behalf of human rights. They require continuous material support, but they do not require any other intervention. They do not require actions or activities that will be provocative. They do not require outside help that could stir up activity which would be deleterious not only to their own growth and to their own future, but which could spark and ignite a catastrophe in the rest of the world.
I have every confidence, and I think those who know the soul and the heart of the Polish people must have confidence, that the Polish people are innovative, are daring, are courageous, that they will evolve a technique, a method, whereby again they will acquire the status in this world that they had in the past. What is not needed at this time is a bickering and a hassle by well-meaning people, well-meaning allies, wellmeaning neighbours who in their enthusiasm to try to help them, may harm them. The people of Poland are of an indomitable spirit and of considerable initiative and drive. I, for one, would rely on that spirit and that support to bring them again the status that is rightfully theirs. What they need is support from every angle, whether it be monetary, or food supplies or the prayers of the people about them. My only thoughts and my only considerations are that we in our enthusiasm help them but not be an obstacle in their way of winning freedom again.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity afforded me by the motion now before the House to participate in this debate on Canada's role and concern in international affairs. 1 had planned to respond to some of the comments made by previous speakers. I was interested in the contribution made by the hon. member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett) in words that were dripping with self-righteousness. I decided otherwise because my hon. friend from Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) responded to those comments in a more gentlemanly manner than I might have done.
1 was interested in the comments made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) regarding the appointment of the member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) to his present position of external affairs critic in the Conservative Party. The minister suggested that the hon. member had become somewhat like a beached whale, beached by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). I would carry that idea just a little further.
I wonder what would have happened to the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, if we were to project that idea a little further. If the hon. member for St. John's West was beached by being placed in the external affairs critic position, perhaps the Prime
Minister (Mr. Trudeau) beached the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville by appointing him as Secretary of State for External Affairs. Possibly to give him a little help, he appointed two other ministers of state and put them in with him to try to help him out of his predicament. Instead of that, the plan has backfired, and he is in a worse situation than ever.
The minister's statement that he had no quarrel with Argentina was a shocking one, in view of the statements that have been made and the charges that have been levied against Argentina, and with every justification for them. For the minister to say we do not have any quarrel with Argentina is almost beyond belief.
It was suggested that the Progressive Conservative Party had an opportunity, when in office for a very short time, to do something about the Argentinian case. The question was raised why we did not cancel the agreement with Argentina then to supply material relating to the CANDU reactor.
The situation was entirely different then, I am sure. At that time Argentina was considered at least a friendly nation in some respects, even though it was far from maintaining those standards of human rights that we would have appreciated. Nevertheless, they had not declared war, they were not at war with one of our NATO allies at that time. There is a war going on now and this government is continuing to supply nuclear fuel bundles to a nation, Argentina, that is fighting against Great Britain at the present moment.
In a somewhat belligerent manner, the minister charged some members of the opposition with voting against the charter of rights. He did not enlarge upon it, but I would like to have asked him where he was when the government refused to incorporate in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms the right to property.
Right on, and human life.

Yes. As my colleague, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), has suggested, the right of human life.
I can remember the time when Canada's role in foreign affairs was considered a very important one, and I remember the time when Canada's voice in the international forum was listened to with respect and appreciation. Those were the days when we had the opportunity to discuss foreign affairs in this House. There were opportunities to debate a whole spectrum of international relationships, Canada's role, Canada's place and Canada's responsibility. But those days seem to have gone. The government places so little importance upon this subject that it will not assume the responsibility of stating on certain occasions that it is prepared to introduce debate on external affairs. I said we used to have those debates, but those days are gone.
In latter years this House has had limited opportunities to deal with the many perplexing problems confronting the international community and where Canada and Canadians stand in relation to those issues. There is little, if any, evidence
June 1, 1982

that there are any fundamental principles upon which our foreign policy is based. Problems are viewed in an indefinite and uncertain fashion, and it has become almost impossible to understand where we are going in our foreign affairs policy and how we propose to get there.
It has been pointed out by other speakers in this debate that the morale in the Department of External Affairs has plummeted, and in spite of a very thorough and logical report commissioned by and submitted to the government, the problems still remain and the recommendations of that report remain in limbo.
Since the present Prime Minister has been in office, there has been a continuing drift in external affairs policy and a downgrading of Canada's Armed Forces, resulting in a serious lack of manpower and equipment. Canada's commitment to NATO has been greatly reduced and, as for NORAD, the Prime Minister has stated that the U.S.A. would not see Canada invaded. I, as well as many other parliamentarians, have had the opportunity to visit the Canadian bases in Europe, and 1 remember very well on different occasions when I had the opportunity to be there what a brave front our service men put on. They were courageous; they were efficient; but as far as their equipment was concerned, we were told it would not stand up in any sense to the rigours of warfare.
Embarrassing.

That is embarrassing to our Armed Forces, it is embarrassing to our Parliament and it is embarrassing to the Canadian people.
The bright spot in recent Canadian history was during the brief period when my party was in office. A comprehensive review of Canada's foreign policy was undertaken with a view to updating the policy in the light of current conditions and restating the principles upon which Canada's commitments would be based.
At that time we stated that the task of Canadian foreign policy in the 1980s was to seek the establishment and maintenance of an international order in which Canada could pursue its own interests and foster its ideals. The goal was to strengthen Canada's voice and actions in the world community in support of the interests of peace and human dignity. Time does not permit the elaboration of those objectives, but I submit the government is derelict in its responsibility by failing to initiate in-depth parliamentary study and debate on these and other important basic principles.
One of our immediate concerns at this moment is the conflict raging on the Falkland Islands, and this forms one of the parts of the motion currently before the House. A crisis was precipitated by the occupation of territory-not theirs- by the armed forces of Argentina. This naked act of aggression is an affront to international law and order and a repudiation of the facts of history. If it is countenanced, it poses a threat to the peace and security of the world.

We are reminded today of the history of this particular crisis and the attitude of Argentina. Argentina has refused to be part of the group which signed the nuclear non-proliferation treaty. Argentina refused to sign the Mexico agreement declaring Latin America as a nuclear free zone. Argentina invaded and occupied territory illegally. Argentina promised Falkland Islanders that their cultural, linguistic and property rights would be respected. That commitment was broken and rights violated, and reports in that connection have been placed before us. Argentina disregarded the UN resolution which condemned Argentina's action and called for Argentina to withdraw. The resolution called upon Argentina to negotiate with Britain to settle their dispute.
Britain accepted that challenge and endeavoured in every way to reach an understanding and a peaceful settlement of this dispute. In fact, Denis Healey, the Labour spokesman in Britain, stated that the Thatcher government had bent over backwards in an endeavour to resolve the crisis. But, of course, Argentina would not respond.
The actions of the European Community have been more forcibly proclaimed than has Canada's commitment. In my view one of the unmistakable indications of our concern and dismay would be at least the halting of any further shipment of nuclear fuel bundles to Argentina until the crisis is resolved. Other actions might be considered, but this should be the minimum. The minister stated that the shipment of such bundles would not affect the war because it possibly would be over before they reached their destination. We have to thank the dock workers who said they would not be a partner in the shipping of those nuclear bundles to Argentina. Apparently they had a great deal more courage than the government in pursuing that course.
I would like just in closing to refer to an article which appeared in my local paper. I see my time has almost gone. This article was written by Mark Rushton and is entitled "Talkin' thru my hat???"-and sometimes he does. However, what he says here is very good.
However, as far as I am concerned, Britain has done the right thing by the Falklands, and by the rest of us in the free world.
If aggressors the world over believe they can get away with scooping minor protectorates like the Falklands or Somalia, what is next. The Russians do not appear at all reluctant to sweep through Europe, gobbling up Afghanistan and Poland.

Mr. Speaker, I apologize for not noticing the Speaker when he rose to call it six o'clock.

Britain, small as she is, is telling the world that western nations are no longer going to sit back and take it.
It is interesting to note that the U.S. is going very public in its support of Britain's action. Where, I wonder is Canada? Still worrying about ensuring its sale of Candu nuclear reactors to Argentina?
Wouldn't it be comforting to know that if a banana republic starts a nuclear war, it is doing it with Canadian products. We may all be dead, but in our graves we will know we have died an employed nation, rich from the sale of such "necessities." Of course, our federal government can protest that it is not selling nuclear weaponry. After all, buyers sign a form saying they won't use their reactors for production of war material.
It is nice, and safe, to be naive, but has Ottawa forgotten the old saying about "All's fair in love and war?"

I hope that this debate will alert the government to some of the problems we face. The time has come to take a new look at our foreign policy and to recognize that in a changing world we must be up to date in order to meet the challenges that confront us from day to day.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this debate today I am tempted to indulge myself in some thoughts about Poland and about the current and possible future state of East-West relations in light of the plight of that hapless country. I am equally tempted to say a word about the Falkland Islands dispute as an expression of the problems of residual remnants of empire and of self-determination in them. These are questions that Canadians might do well to ponder and to make such contribution to their resolution as their resources and interests may determine.
However, I have been asked whether I would instead say something about the third part of the opposition motion which relates to the royal commission on conditions of foreign service. I am happy to do so not only because I was in the foreign service for some 12 years, but because during that time 1 had the opportunity to work closely with the royal commissioner, Pam McDougall, in Vietnam. 1 recall very well the adverse circumstances in which we served in Saigon and Hanoi and the frustrations of attempting to be a peacemaker. The gospel says blessed is the peacemaker; I would suggest that more often the peace-maker is frustrated, and we certainly had good measure of that.
Miss McDougall has personal experience of life in the foreign service, including at smaller posts where Canadian
interests are sometimes not so obvious as in larger. She has offered the government and indeed the people of Canada a timely review. It is in some respects similar to those which emerged in recent years in other western countries, such as the Duncan report in the United Kingdom and several reviews in France and the United States.
It is hardly surprising that from time to time such reports, including the McDougall report, are prepared. They offer useful benchmarks in the continuing reevaluation of our diplomatic service. Change has accelerated in international relations, as in so much else. It is certainly appropriate for Canadians to consider upon occasion what changes should be made in the conditions of foreign service, to match the differing circumstances in which diplomats find themselves today.
As technology continues to annihilate space and limit the influence of time, diplomacy finds itself excluded from variety of functions which traditionally fell to it because of the distances between states and the time it took to consult amongst them. Indeed, diplomats today live in a different world where the ease and rapidity of travel and telecommunications, the omnipresent press, the pervasive influence of television, the increasing emphasis on multilateral diplomacy as opposed to traditional bilateral diplomacy, and a variety of other factors, have made for different circumstances in all foreign services today. Additionally, contacts between countries at a variety of levels, through a range of non-governmental organizations, have also contributed to the new circumstances in which our diplomats must work. It is a long way, Mr. Speaker, from the world of Lord Dufferin or even Lawrence Durrell, or the Canadian diplomat Charles Ritchie who has described so wittily the role of Canada on the world stage in the post-war years. That role was in several major respects fundamentally different from what we see today.
Canada, during the immediate post-war years, was a middle power playing a significant role on a relatively uncrowded stage. Canada had emerged from a self-imposed isolation to the giddy experience of world diplomacy. In the few decades since then Canada's role has changed, and if our foreign service does not also evolve, some of our diplomats may find applicable to themselves the unenviable description offered by Anthony Sampson, a noted British writer who said:
The intensity and isolation of embassy life and entertainment ... the formalities and protocol, all contribute to the diplomat's lassitude. Young British diplomats soon lose their curiosity, usually after their third posting, and achieve a lacklustre expression, an immunity to new experience and new people, and above all an absence of zeal.
That situation is characteristic of a foreign service attempting to carry out policies which are either not clearly enunciated or else irrelevant to the real national interests of the country involved. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in Canada there is no need for this. The challenge for Canadian policy is to pursue our own particular interests, in new and evolving areas, new in the sense of emphasis rather than principle. The challenges are
June I, 1982

also new in the sense of more emphasis on trade, not merely in the more traditional practice of tariff negotiations, but in removing and reducing non-tariff barriers, of new initatives in the energy field and telecommunications, in the elimination of pollution, and in promoting a regime of law for the oceans of the world. All these and other activities represent a new emphasis for the Canadian foreign service, roles which no other entity in our society can possibly play.
Some reference has been made to the role of newspapers in providing some of the information on which governments formulate their foreign policy, and on which governments act. But I would suggest that no newspaper can represent our particular interests to another nation. Mr. Pearson made an observation, some years prior to that of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), to the effect that newspapers are often well informed, their foreign correspondents are well informed. They cannot, however, provide the representation of Canadian interests, nor indeed can they evaluate knowledge of the local country policies against our interests. One challenge for Canadian policymakers is to be certain of our own interests and to avoid spreading our resources too thinly. Over-staffing is to be avoided in any organization. Indeed, there are some who would argue that today we have too many posts abroad, we have too many missions not fulfilling a useful function. In that respect I would bear in mind the admonition Arthur Andrew, a distinguished Canadian foreign service officer who wrote:
An effective foreign service cannot be obtained simply by spending a lot of money and maintaining a large variety of diplomatic missions. The diplomat is extremely conscious of the expense and inconvenience of maintaining him abroad and he is quick to know if his work is important or not. It is normal for him to think that the foreign ministry at home does not give proper weight to the importance of his work. He accepts this and goes on trying to convert his colleagues at home to his way of thinking. But he cannot function and may become a parody diplomat if he comes to believe that his job has no significance. There are undoubtedly many diplomatic posts in the world for which there is little or no present justification. Maintaining them may be inescapable but can have a devastating effect on the diplomats who are obliged to keep them open.
Indeed, the challenge for Canadians, the Canadian government, and the foreign service is to continue to employ our talent, of which there is a vast reservoir in our foreign service, in imaginative ways, helping to ensure that members of the foreign service have the direct challenge of contributing to the formulation of our foreign policy. If some posts require a reduction in staff, there are certainly others which could benefit from strengthening of their activities, particularly in the trade field.
On another subject, Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether, in the circumstances of the foreign service today, or indeed at any time, the introduction of collective bargaining or, in effect, the trade union method of negotiating conditions of employment has been a very helpful innovation.
Without wanting to sound like an ultra-traditionalist, I would suggest that we have not benefited much from the introduction into the foreign service of collective bargaining. I would certainly hope that at least some of the more difficult manifestations of collective bargaining can be avoided by
Supply
ensuring that the practices and conditions within the foreign service are such as not to trigger that particular form of redress.
In that context, of course, the report of the royal commission becomes particularly relevant since Miss McDougall has attempted, with considerable success, to address some of the problems of the foreign service in an environment where, for example, the role of spouses is changing, or where singleparent families have particular constraints or needs. I hope that members of the House will take the trouble to review some of the recommendations which Miss McDougall has offered because they have real validity. In that connection I would note that the Prime Minister has requested the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) to assume responsibility for the review of the report's recommendations. In carrying out that role, the minister has appointed a senior member of the department to co-ordinate a response which is now well advanced.
